title: DPA pseudonymization standards and verification checklist
content:
Purpose:
This draft is intended to be an annex to customer DPAs that defines minimum pseudonymization standards for vendors processing Redwood customer data in inference and telemetry contexts, and a practical verification checklist for security reviewers and legal teams. It is meant for inclusion in commercial DPAs and vendor onboarding exhibits where residual inference logs or non-production copies of query data may be retained or used for quality/improvement activities.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to any vendor or subprocessor that: stores, analyzes, or otherwise processes query text, prompts, embeddings, or model outputs that are reasonably linkable to an identifiable person or organisation.
- Covers: inference logs, short-term KV/prefix caches, telemetry events with user identifiers, dataset snapshots created for troubleshooting, and derived training/eval corpora.
- Does not replace sector-specific regulatory controls (HIPAA, PCI) but sets a baseline that must be augmented where those regulations apply.

Key definitions (for contract language):
- Pseudonymized data: data that has undergone technical transformations such that identifiers have been replaced or obscured, and additional information required to re-identify is kept separately under technical and organisational controls.
- Reversible pseudonymization: transformations where a mapping table or key exists that can reconstruct original identifiers; requires strict key management and audit controls.
- Irreversible pseudonymization: tokenisation or cryptographic hashing with salt or one-way functions where reconstruction is computationally infeasible for the vendor.

Minimum pseudonymization obligations (contract clause language suggestions):
1) Identification and classification: the vendor must classify all incoming data according to the Redwood Data Classification Matrix and flag any records containing direct identifiers before retention.
2) Transformation requirement: before persisting or exporting logs containing direct identifiers, the vendor must apply at least one of the following:
   - deterministic tokenization with an industry-standard HSM-backed key (reversible) OR
   - salted cryptographic hashing with per-customer salt and documented algorithm (irreversible) OR
   - field-level redaction for high-risk attributes with a documented rationale (irreversible).
3) Key management: keys used for reversible pseudonymization must be stored in a customer-or-vendor-managed KMS that supports access logging, rotation every 90 days, and emergency key revocation.
4) Metadata separation: metadata that can re-link pseudonymized records (customer ids, session tokens) must be stored separately, with access controls and logging that meet Redwood's least-privilege and MFA requirements.
5) Minimal retention: pseudonymized datasets used for model tuning or analytics may be retained only for the period agreed in the DPA annex; default retention must not exceed 90 days without explicit written permission.
6) No re-identification: vendor shall not perform or outsource any re-identification attempt on pseudonymized data except when explicitly requested in writing by Redwood for investigatory purposes; such requests require a signed, scoped exception and audit logging.

Verification and evidence checklist (for procurement and security review):
- Evidence: sample logs showing transformation pipeline (redacted) and a diagram of data flows with pseudonymization points annotated.
- Code artefacts: links to the repository or PR implementing pseudonymization with brief README that maps algorithms to endpoints.
- Key management proof: screenshots or audit export showing KMS keys, rotation schedule, and access grant records for the relevant service account.
- Retention proof: storage lifecycle policy or object lifecycle config (e.g., S3 lifecycle) showing automatic deletion/expiration.
- Access controls: IAM policies and a list of human/service principals with access; demonstration of least privilege and MFA enforcement for high-risk roles.
- Test re-identification attempt: supply an internal Red-team test (safe, scoped) report showing that vendor cannot re-identify a small test set without access to separated metadata/keys.
- Incident handling: a sample incident playbook that includes steps for emergency key revocation, dataset sequester, and notification to Redwood security/legal.

Operational notes and acceptable techniques (engineering-focused guidance):
- Prefer irreversible approaches where customer use-cases allow (irreversible = simpler audit surface).
- If reversible tokenisation is required for debugging, require ephemeral keys with minimum TTL and per-customer scoping.
- Salted hashing: use per-customer salts stored in KMS; document algorithms (e.g., HMAC-SHA256 with 32-byte salt). Avoid unauthenticated simple hashes for any high-risk fields.
- Store transformation logs (who/what/when) for at least 180 days for forensic capability.

Audit cadence and rights:
- Redwood or our designated auditor has the right to one on-site or remote evidence review per 12 months, and the right to ad hoc reviews after any security incident.
- Vendor must provide requested artefacts within 10 business days.
- For high-risk integrations, consider a tabletop and a small sample forensic exercise before production cutover.

Exception handling and escalation:
- Any deviation from these standards requires an exception request submitted to Redwood security with justification, impact assessment, and compensating controls.
- Temporary exceptions (<=30 days) may be approved by the engineering security manager with automatic expiry; longer exceptions require legal sign-off.

Template clause (contract-ready language snippet):
"Vendor shall implement and maintain, at its own cost, pseudonymization measures for any Customer Data classified as 'identifiable' prior to storing or exporting such data for analysis or model improvement. Such measures shall include, at a minimum, either (i) reversible tokenization managed with KMS-backed keys under strict access controls, or (ii) irreversible salted hashing using per-customer salts. Vendor shall document algorithms, key lifecycle, and data flow diagrams and produce evidence in Section X upon request. Vendor shall not re-identify pseudonymized Customer Data except when expressly authorized by Customer in writing and under documented controls."

Practical onboarding checklist (short action list for vendor onboarding):
- Submit data flow diagram with pseudonymization points.
- Provide code link/PR and brief implementation notes.
- Produce KMS access audit exports and rotation evidence.
- Configure storage lifecycle to auto-delete pseudonymized snapshots after agreed period.
- Run a scoped re-identification test and submit results.
- Accept audit rights and produce SOC/ISO evidence where available.

Notes to reviewers (internal):
- TODO: align retention defaults with product teams (current 90-day placeholder).
- TODO: confirm whether per-customer salt requirement is feasible for dedicated vendors with a single shared tenant design.
- See linked artifacts for prior discussions and a reference PR implementing a prototype transformation library.

End of draft.
